newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Q4 better time for Singapore electronics - Fraser.
newsitem.headline: Q4 better time for Singapore electronics - Fraser.

text.p: Negative sentiment could hit the Singapore electronics sector between now and September, but the longer-term outlook is brighter, a report by Fraser-AMMB Research said.
"Though PC demand is expected to pick up again by fall, we except sentiment towards the sector to be impacted negatively between now and September," said the report, issued last week.
It said a premium price-earnings rating for the sector is not likely to emerge until clearer signs of a demand pick-up resurface, which it expected to take place in the fourth quarter.
Fraser said weaker-than-expected current quarter earnings by Intel and Seagate should not badly affect the Singapore electronics industry.

"Based on indications from the industry, we do not believe the Singapore electronics sector will be severely impacted as the apparent slowdown in demand is linked to seasonal reasons and product transition issues," it said.
It added that the warnings were not alarming except for those who focus on quarter-to-quarter results.
"Despite the apparent slowdown, growth in PC sales in 1997 should still match 1996's growth rate of 18 percent," it said.
Demand from emerging economies will be a key factor for demand in coming years.
"With rapid economic development, the Chinese PC market offers tremendous potential given an extremely low PC ownership of one PC per 245 people versus one PC per 6.7 people in the U.S."
Fraser-AMMB Research also forecast a pick-up in the hard disk drive sector for the fourth quarter.
Further, it added that the semicondutor cycle was turning up, with strong expectations for 1998.

"After contracting 8.6 percent last year as a result of a collapse in DRAM prices, the global semiconductor industry is expected to recover 4.6 percent in 1997, and thereafter to grow more than 20 percent per annum to year 2000," it said.
Electronic parts and components account for nearly 60 percent of Singapore's total exports and about 25 percent of gross domestic product.
Local production, however, has been crimped lately because of a slump in global electronics.
